name: United Arab Emirates
governanceModel: State-directed strategy, recently consolidated under a single new AI Authority
debateTopics: Consolidating AI governance under a single new Authority
Chip access diplomacy and the shift toward unrestricted export status
overview:
The UAE consolidated its AI governance in June 2026, approving a new Artificial Intelligence and Data Authority that merges the former Office of AI/Digital Economy/Remote Work Applications, the UAE Data Office, and the TDRA's digital-government portfolio into one body. Omar Sultan Al Olama, the UAE's Minister of State for AI since 2017, was confirmed as its chair — extending his existing mandate into a single, consolidated institution. (Whether the Authority has completed its formal legal and operational stand-up beyond this June 2026 approval has not been independently confirmed.)

On the industry side, Abu Dhabi's G42 (valued at roughly $20B in one April 2026 estimate) and the Technology Innovation Institute jointly produce the Falcon model family, including 2026 releases Falcon Perception (efficient multimodal) and Falcon-H1 Arabic, described by TII and several outlets as the world's leading Arabic-language LLM. Chip access, once a genuine point of friction, moved further toward resolution in mid-2026: after the US authorized G42 to purchase up to 35,000 NVIDIA Blackwell chips in November 2025, the US Commerce Department reclassified the UAE into the highest-trust Export Administration Regulations tier (Country Group A:5) on July 10, 2026, removing the requirement for individual export licenses for approved UAE entities — including G42 — to receive NVIDIA Blackwell and AMD Instinct chips. Legal analyses of the underlying rule note that this license-free treatment for G42 and its Core42 cloud unit is, per Supplement No. 8 to Part 740, a roughly 270-day pre-approval window rather than a permanent exemption, unless those entities become US-headquartered within that period.

currentDirection.summary: The UAE is consolidating institutional control over AI policy under a single new Authority chaired by Omar Sultan Al Olama, AI minister since 2017 — a centralising move even though no binding AI-specific law has followed — alongside continued state investment in sovereign compute and Arabic-language frontier models, and a July 2026 US export-control reclassification that eased the UAE's access to advanced AI chips.

debates.topic: Consolidating AI governance under a single new Authority
debates.summary: Merging three previously separate federal bodies into one Authority centralises AI policy, which initial coverage frames as a significant institutional bet on unified control.
debates.expanded: Combining the AI office, Data Office, and TDRA's digital-government functions gives the new Authority broad reach across data governance, AI development, and remote-work policy. Supporters see this as removing coordination friction between previously siloed bodies; the concentration of power in one authority under one minister is itself a notable governance choice worth watching as it beds in. Whether the Authority has completed its formal legal and operational stand-up beyond the June 2026 approval has not been independently confirmed.

debates.topic: Chip access diplomacy and the shift toward unrestricted export status
debates.summary: The US eased chip-export restrictions on the UAE twice within about eight months — approving a major Blackwell sale to G42 in late 2025, then reclassifying the UAE into the highest-trust export control tier in July 2026 — substantially narrowing, though perhaps not eliminating, earlier friction over advanced-hardware access.
debates.expanded: The November 2025 approval for G42 to purchase up to 35,000 NVIDIA Blackwell chips was a major reversal of prior US reluctance, tied to Gulf 'compute diplomacy' and multibillion-dollar investment pledges. Earlier 2026 analysis had argued that US export rules still kept the UAE in an 'AI technology slow lane' in some respects. That picture changed materially on July 10, 2026, when the US Commerce Department reclassified the UAE from Export Administration Regulations Country Groups D:3/D:4 into Country Group A:5 — the highest trust tier — removing the requirement for individual export licenses for approved UAE entities, including G42, to receive NVIDIA Blackwell and AMD Instinct chips. Law-firm analyses of the final rule (Morgan Lewis, Akin Gump) note an important qualification, however: G42 and its Core42 cloud unit's license-free status under Supplement No. 8 to Part 740 is reported to be a roughly 270-day pre-approval window rather than an open-ended exemption, unless they become US-headquartered entities within that period. How this conditional framework operates in practice, and whether it is extended or made permanent, remains to be seen.

notableGaps.note: No dedicated, independent UAE-based AI-policy think tank was identified in this audit. Adjacent bodies exist — Dubai's 'Think AI' initiative (a government-EY convening on AI policy) and an Abu Dhabi 'AI Centre of Excellence' oriented more toward research and commercialization — but neither reads as a traditional policy think tank, so this may reflect a genuine gap or simply incomplete search coverage.

Coverage of the UAE's July 2026 export-control reclassification often describes G42's license-free access to advanced AI chips as settled, but law-firm analyses of the underlying BIS rule (Supplement No. 8 to Part 740) indicate this status for G42 and Core42 is a time-limited pre-approval window (roughly 270 days) rather than a permanent exemption, unless they become US-headquartered within that period.
